claims.text: The word pattachitra comes from the Sanskrit patta, a painted piece of cloth or a plate, and chitra, meaning paintings or picture.

quotes.quote: The word Pattachitra is derived from the Sanskrit word "patta", which means a painted piece of cloth,or a plate;chitra means paintings or picture
Pata has been derived from the Sanskrit word 'Patta'
Derived from the Sanskrit word patta (canvas) and chitra (painting)

claims.text: Patta painting, or patta chitra, is one of the typical regional arts of the coastal state of Orissa in eastern India.

quotes.quote: or patta chitra, is one of the typical regional arts of the coastal state of Orissa in eastern India

claims.text: Patta painting in Orissa focuses on the Hindu epics, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, and on the Jagannath cult in particular.

quotes.quote: the Hindu epics in general, the Mahabharata and the Ramayana, and the Jagannath cult in particular
So far patta painting of Orissa have adhered to only religious sentiments and mostly depict topics related to Krishnalila and Jagannath.

claims.text: Traditionally patta painting was practised only by the Chitrakara caste as their caste occupation.

quotes.quote: Traditionally it was prac tised only by the Chitrakara caste as their caste occupation.

claims.text: Pattachitra paintings were traditionally drawn by the Mahapatra or Maharanas, described as the original artiste caste in Odisha.

quotes.quote: Pattachitra paintings were traditionally drawn by the Mahapatra or maharanas, the original artiste caste in Odisha.
Artisans of 'Pattchitra' belong to the 'Mahapatra' or 'Maharanas' caste and live across the various cities of Orisha.

claims.text: The GI application calls the canvas, the patta astra, the most important feature of pattachitra, without which the art's significance is incomplete.

quotes.quote: The most important feature of pattachitra is the canvas on which the painting is done, without this base, called patta astra the significance of the art is incomplete.

claims.text: Patta painting is a family or household craft whose procedures are carried out by different members of the same household.

quotes.quote: patta painting is a family or household craft. All of the procedures involved in patta painting are carried out by different members of the same household.
The artists and his family together perform these steps

claims.text: Brightly coloured pattachitra works were produced at Puri as souvenirs for the pilgrims of the Jagannath temple.

quotes.quote: The brillinantly colored patachitra works were pr oduced at puri or souveriers for the pilgrims of the Jaganath temple.
Workshops producing devotional paintings for pilgrims prospered around the temple in Puri.

claims.text: The GI application argues that pattachitra's primitive style and its role in temple services, contemporary with the 12th-century building of the Jagannath temple, suggest an early date for its origin.

quotes.quote: The proof of origin of the "Pattachitra" art can be traced from their primitive style and the important role it plays in temple services which are contemporary with the building of the Jagannath temple (12th century)
All this suggests an early date for its origin.

claims.text: According to the GI application, pata paintings flourished in Orissa in the early 15th and 16th centuries.

quotes.quote: These paintings flourished in Orissa in early 15 th 16th centuries.

claims.text: The GI application says the cult of Jagannath used pata paintings to spread the faith throughout Orissa and beyond, through the patronage of the Jagannath temple.

quotes.quote: The cult of Jagannath used Pata paintings to spread the faith throughout Orissa and also outside b ecause of the patronage by the temple of Jagannath

claims.text: According to the GI application, Chitrakaras painted Jagannath patas in large numbers, and these slowly outnumbered paintings on other themes in Orissa.

quotes.quote: Chitrakaras (the painters) painted Jagannath Patas in large number and slowly these Patas outnumbered other thematic ones in Orissa

claims.text: Every year on Jyeshtha purnima the ritual bathing discolours the painted wooden images of Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra, which are repainted over 15 days while absent from the inner sanctuary.

quotes.quote: Every year on Jyeshtha purnima, the painted wooden images of Jaganath, Balabhadra and their sister Subhadra are ritually deansed with holy waters.
This bathing discolors the icons and they are removed from the temple for 15 days so that they can be repainted.
so that the images are kept in the anasara ghara for repainting for fifteen days
when the images are ab sent from the ratna singhasana (the inner sanctuary)

claims.text: While the images are away, three patta paintings of the trinity are kept in the main shrine as their proxies; these are called anasara patti.

quotes.quote: During this time, the three"Patachitra paintings" depicting the divine trio are substituted for the images by the temple painter.
three large patta paintings of the trinity are kept inside the main shrine, as proxies of them
These paintings are called anasara patti.
Initially, patachitra was called anasar patti in reference to the fifteen-day ritual period known as anasara or anavasra
In this period known as 'anasara', they are substituted by majestic paintings that represent them.

claims.text: Other patta paintings worshipped in the Jagannath temple include the krishna patti, bamana patti and kandarpa patti, so patta painting is needed for rituals throughout the year.

quotes.quote: other patta paintings worshipped in the temple on various occasions include the krishna patti
the bamana patti, a painting of Bamana
and the kandarpa patti, paintings of Kandarpa worshipped on the twelfth and thirteen days
patta painting is an im portant part of the Jagannath cult and is required in one fonn or other for temple rituals throughout the year

claims.text: According to the Jagannath temple chronicle, Chitrakaras were first brought to Puri by Anangabhima Deva II to do the temple's painting, and given tax-free lands.

quotes.quote: According to the Jagannath temple chronicle, they were first brought to Puri by the emperor Anangabhima Deva II to carry out all the painting required for the temple, which gave Chitrakara families tax-free lands.

claims.text: The image of Jagannath is carved of margosa wood and painted by Chitrakaras, who were brought to Puri from various places as servants of Jagannath.

quotes.quote: The image of Jagannath is carved out of mar gosa wood and painted by members of the Chitrakara caste, who were brought to Puri from various places as the servants of Jagannath.

claims.text: Chitrakara society is divided into three badas named after the trinity, which supply the anasara pattis and colour the images and their cars for the Car festival.

quotes.quote: Chitrakara society is subdivided into three groups or badas named after the deities of the trinity
supplying the respective anasara pattis, colouring the images and their cars on the occasion of the Car festival

claims.text: In the remote past primed paper was the base of the painting, and in course of time the Chitrakaras used primed cloth as the base.

quotes.quote: In the remote past, primed paper was used as the base of the painting.
In course of time, the Chitrakaras used primed cloth as the base or canvas for the painting work.

claims.text: Jatripattis, paintings meant exclusively for pilgrims, were taken home as souvenirs of the pilgrimage and worshipped there as representatives of the trinity.

quotes.quote: Jatripatti (painting meant exclusively for pilgrims)
who used to take these paintings back with them as souvenirs of the pilgrimage. They also used to worship these at home as representatives of the trinity.

claims.text: A V&A painting on cloth of the Jagannatha temple in the Orissan style, dated 1670, was most probably executed at Puri and sent to Nepal.

quotes.quote: This painting on cloth (pata), done in the Orissan style, depicts the famous Jagannatha Temple in Puri, Orissa.
although it was most probably executed at Puri, it was sent to Nepal to mark a festival ritual performed by the ruler of Bhaktapur
in the year Samvat 790 (= 1670)

claims.text: The same V&A record's brief description says this 1670 Jagannatha temple painting was painted in Bhaktapur, Nepal, in gouache on cotton.

quotes.quote: Painting, Jagannatha temple at Puri, painted in Bhaktapur, Nepal, gouache on cotton, 1670

claims.text: After a two-year INTACH research project from 1998 to 2000, Raghurajpur was selected as the first heritage village of Odisha.

quotes.quote: After two years of Research Projects from 1998 to 2000 by INTACH, the village has selected as the first heritage village of Odisha
In 2000, the Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural Heritage (INTACH) declared Raghurajpur a 'heritage village,'
Raghurajpur was recognized as a Heritage Village in 2000.
In 2000, after a two-year research and documentation project by INTACH, starting in 1998, the village of Raghurajpur was chosen to be developed as Odisha's first village of cultural significance.

claims.text: Outlook Traveller writes that Raghurajpur was once known as keeper of Odisha's pattachitra largely due to the late Jagannath Mohapatra, winner of the President of India's award in 1965, who lived there.

quotes.quote: Once known as the keepers of Odisha's ancient pattachitra art, largely due to the late Jagannath Mohapatra (winner of the President of India's award in 1965) who lived here

claims.text: Mythologically the Chitrakaras are believed to be the descendants of Biswakarma, the celestial architect of the Hindus.

quotes.quote: Mythologically the Chitrakaras are believed to be the descendants of Biswakarma, the celestial architect of the Hindus

claims.text: Scholars cited by Gulf News suggest pattachitra dates back to the 2nd century BCE, to mural art in the Khandagiri and Udayagiri caves of Bhubaneswar.

quotes.quote: Scholars suggest that pattachitra dates back to the 2nd century BCE to the mural art found inside Khandagiri and Udayagiri caves of Bhubaneshwar

claims.text: It is said that pattachitra in its modern form dates back to the construction of the Jagannath temple in the 12th century.

quotes.quote: It is said that the modern day version of pattachitra dates back to the time of construction of Lord Jagannath Temple in 12th century AD
It is said that the pattachitra of Odisha dates back to the 12th century

claims.text: The artists themselves say the name comes from the remote past, when painting was done with a brush of locally available screw-pine wood called patta.

quotes.quote: According to the artists themselves, in the remote past paint ing was done with a brush prepared from locally available screw-pine wood called patta.

claims.text: The GI application gives four steps in order: preparation of patta, preparation of pigments, motif selection and layout, and finally painting.

quotes.quote: which are preparation of patta, preparation of pigments, motif selection and layout, and finally painting
The steps are: 1 Preparation of patta , 2 Preparation of Pigments, 3 Motif selection , 4 Painting

claims.text: The canvas is made by pasting layers of old, used cotton cloth, such as saris or dhotis, together with tamarind glue.

quotes.quote: In Orissa, the canvas is prepared by pasting layers of old and used cloth with the help of tamarind glue.
To prepare a patti on handmade canvas, the artists use, old and used cotton cloth and tamarind seed gum.
This canvas was prepared by applying tamarind glue (prepared from tamarind seeds) and chalk solution on clean cotton saris or dhotis in two or three layers.
Artisans take a few old well-washed saris to prepare a canvas.

claims.text: The first layer of cloth is spread on the floor or on a hensa mat, and the glue is applied over it in the manner of smearing cow dung.

quotes.quote: The first layer of cloth is spread on the cemented floor or on a mat (Hensa), over which gum is applied on the manner of smearing cowdung
The glue is applied over it in the manner of smearing cow dung on the floor of a house.

claims.text: A second layer of cloth is pasted over the first, the bubbles and patches of glue between the layers are removed, and a third and fourth layer are added if needed.

quotes.quote: The second layer of cloth is spread over it and pasted together. The bubbles and patches of glue in between the layers are removed.
If need arises a third and fourth layer are also used.

claims.text: The pasted canvas is left to dry in the sun, taken off the floor, rolled and preserved, and canvases are prepared in large numbers especially in winter and summer or spring.

quotes.quote: Now this is left in the sun to dry. When it is dried, it is taken of the floor, rolled and preserved for painting.
Especially during winter and summer or spring, these canvases are prepared in large numbers and are stored.

claims.text: For the glue, tamarind seeds are crushed on a sila stone, soaked in water in an earthen pot for half a day, ground to a thick paste and cooked.

quotes.quote: The tamarind seeds are crushed on a sila and then soaked in water in an earthen pot for half a day. Then they are grounded and made into thick liquid. This liquid is cooked to obtain the glue.

Seeds are crushed on a flat stone bed (sila), then soaked in water in an earthen pot for half a day. Then they are ground and made into thick paste, which is cooked with required water to obtain the gum.

claims.text: Tripathy describes insect-free tamarind seeds soaked overnight, ground to pulp, mixed 1:2 with water and heated for 30-45 minutes until sticky and semi-solid.

quotes.quote: insect-free, good-quality seeds are soaked in water overnight and are then made into pulp by grinding
The pulp is then mixed with water in a 1:2 ratio and is kept on the hearth for 30-45 minutes until it be comes sticky and semi-solid.

claims.text: Kiran Pradeep writes that the tamarind seeds are crushed and soaked for 4-5 days until soft, then boiled in water to make the glue.

quotes.quote: tamarind seeds are crushed and soaked for 4-5 days to become soft. After they become soft they are boiled in water and made into glue.

claims.text: In the GI application's account the housewives carry out the entire process of making the gum and preparing the patta.

quotes.quote: The housewives execute the entire process of making the gum and preparing the patta.

claims.text: Tripathy found women usually making the tamarind glue and chalk solution and smoothing the surface, while men applied the glue and chalk solution to the cloth.

quotes.quote: Preparation of the tamarind glue and the chalk-powder solution, as well as smooth ing the surface, are usually done by the women
while the preparation of the can vas itself, that is, the application of tamarind glue and chalk-powder solution to the cotton cloth, is carried out by the men

claims.text: The khadi coating is made by mixing tamarind glue with chalk, generally in equal proportions of fifty percent each.

quotes.quote: b. Application of Khadi (Khadi Lagi) The coating is obtained by mixing tamarind glue with chalk in the proper proportions. Generally the proportion of chalk and glue is fifty percent each.
The coating is obtained by mixing tamarind gum with chalk in proportion of 50 - 50

claims.text: Tripathy describes khadi pathara chalk ground fine and mixed 1:2 with water, then made sticky with 400 gm of tamarind glue per kg of chalk powder.

quotes.quote: a white chalk locally called khadi pathara is ground to a fine powder and mixed well with water in a 1:2 ratio. To make it sticky 400 gm of tamarind glue is mixed together with I kg of chalk powder.

claims.text: Two or three coats of chalk solution are applied to both sides of the patti, drying between coats, which also reduces the colour used in painting.

quotes.quote: a solution of chalk powder is applied on both the sides with a piece of cloth and left to dry. Two or three such coatings of chalk solution are ap plied, with an interval for drying each time
to make the canvas more perfect and thus reduce the amount of colour consumed in painting

claims.text: The GI application says that when the first coat is a bit dry it is rubbed with round soft stones called barada or jhuna barada, the first phase of rubbing with jhuna barada.

quotes.quote: When the first coat becomes a bit dry, it is rubbed with round soft stones called barada or jhuna barada.
The first phase of rubbing is done with jhuna barada and the subsequent smoothing is done with chikana barada.

claims.text: The Orissa Review describes the barada used to rub the khadi coat, once it is a bit dry, as an agate stone.

quotes.quote: When Khadi becomes a bit dry, it is rubbed with agate stone called 'barada'.

claims.text: Two types of barada are used, a rough khadada barada and a fine chikana barada, and the Orissa Review and Tripathy have the rough stone do the first rubbing.

quotes.quote: Two types of baradas are used. The rough one is called khadada barada
Two types of barada is used - Khadada barada (rough) chikana barada (fine). The first phase of rubbing is done withkhadada barada and the subsequent smoothing is done with chikana barada.
first with a rough surfaced stone called bagada barada, and then with a comparatively smooth and polished stone called chikkana barada

claims.text: The rubbing, locally called pattighasa, is done systematically with horizontal and vertical movements on both sides of the pati, which otherwise becomes shaky and twisted, until the surface is completely polished and fit to be painted.

quotes.quote: Rubbing is done systematically by horizontal and vertical movements.
Rubbing and polishing are done on the both sides of pati otherwise it becomes shaky and twisted.
that is, smoothing the canvas, which is 10cally called a pattighasa
till the surface of the canvas becomes completely polished and fit to be painted

claims.text: After coating and polishing, the patis are trimmed and cut to size with scissors, called kainchi, and patis for ganjapa with a ssama, a round iron rim with a sharp edge attached to a log.

quotes.quote: c. Sizing (Sama-Nakariva) After the coats are applied and polished the patis are trimmed on the sides and are cut into required sizes with the help of scissors.
Kainchi - scissors is used to cut the patis into required sizes.
Patis for ganjapa are cut by the help of ssama (a round iron rim with a sharp edge attached to a log)

claims.text: For tussar silk paintings, the silk is pasted onto a board of the required size and dried before painting.

quotes.quote: Required size of ply wood board is taken on which silk fabric is pasted with the help of Fevicol and then it is allowed to dry.
The cloth is first fixed tightly and evenly on a wooden slate or slab with the help of glue around its border, after which it is painted.

claims.text: For white, a paste of crushed conch shell is kept with water in an earthen pot, the rough portion that settles is thrown away, and the rest is filtered.

quotes.quote: The conch shells are crushed and ground and made into a paste. This is kept in an earthen pot, mixed with water.
After a few hours of storing the sedemented water comes up and khadada (rough) portion goes down the pot and is thrown away. Now the whole substance is filtered

claims.text: In Tripathy's account the conch shells are ground into tiny pieces and soaked, and the pulp is boiled twice or more to obtain the white.

quotes.quote: White is prepared from conch shells, which are ground into very tiny pieces and soaked with water. This pulp is then boiled twice or more to obtain the white colour.
White is prepared from crushed, boiled, and filtered shells.
First of all, Artisans grind it and make powder. Then boil it by adding water as required. In the next process, they strain and filter the paste.

claims.text: Crude cinnabar is levigated in a mortar with sugar water or lime juice and the yellowish water drained off, fifteen times or more for the purest, then mixed with gum, formed into tablets and dried.

quotes.quote: The crude cinnabar is thoroughly levigated in a mortar with the help of sugar water or limejuice, which is a better substitute. Then the cinnabar is allowed to settle and the yellowish water is carefully drained off.

The process is repeated fifteen times or even more to obtain the purest cinnabar. It is again levigated with sugared water or limejuice and gum and after being thoroughly mixed it is formed into tablets and dried.

claims.text: Red clay or gairika is pulverised on stone for one whole day, and the colour is then obtained by washing it in pure water.

quotes.quote: Red clay or gairika is pulverized on stone for one whole day and thereafter the color is obtained by washing it in pure water.

claims.text: Black is oil wick lamp black, collected from inside an earthen pot put over the oil lamp, where the black from the wick sticks.

quotes.quote: It is obtained from oil wick lamp black. An earthen pot is put over the oil lamp. The black from the wick gets stuck inside the pot.
Black is made out of lampblack

claims.text: Tripathy records black prepared by mixing the soot of a kerosene lamp with locally available polanga or coconut oil.

quotes.quote: Black is prepared by mixing the soot of a kerosene lamp with locally available polanga or coconut oil.

claims.text: Cinnabar, yellow and ochre are ground from minerals to fine powder and mixed with water and a little elephant-apple extract until even and uniform.

quotes.quote: Cinnabar, yellow, and ochre are prepared from different minerals, which are ground to fine powder before water is added, along with a little extract from the elephant-apple tree in different proportions for the different colours, the whole being mixed well until it becomes even and uniform.

claims.text: In the Puri-area method painting starts by marking the border, a narrow space in from the edge of the pati, with a scale and ruler.

quotes.quote: we are going to discuss the popular method followed by thechitrakaras of Puri area.
It starts with the demarcation of the border leaving a narrow space around from the last edge of the pati, with the help of scale and ruler.
It is a tradition to complete the borders of the painting first.

claims.text: The painter makes the rough sketch directly with the brush in light red and yellow, without pencil or charcoal for the preliminary drawing.

quotes.quote: The artist does not use a pencil or charcoal for the preliminary drawings.
The painter then starts making a rough sketch directly with the brush using light red and yellow.

claims.text: One artist told Gulf News that the painter sketches the bare outlines with charcoal or limestone, usually from memory.

quotes.quote: The painter sketches the bare outlines of the painting with charcoal or limestone. This is usually done from memory

claims.text: The sketch, done without details such as eyes, nose and fingers, is generally drawn by the master craftsman at the head of the family.

quotes.quote: After this sketching is done without going into details like, eye, nose, lips, fingers etc.
Generally the master craftsman on the head of the family draws it.

claims.text: Swarajya describes the master painter outlining the anasara pati figure with a thin brush dipped in red hingula, a base sketch known as the tipana.

quotes.quote: With a thin brush dipped in red hingula, he deftly outlines the figure of Jagannath in all detail. This is the base sketch, or what is known as the tipana.

claims.text: After sketching, the background is coloured first; red backgrounds are the most common in Orissa pattachitra, and traditionally cinnabar was the usual background colour.

quotes.quote: Sketching is followed by colouring, and here comes the background first.
the red background in pattachitra of Orissa is the most common
Traditionally cinnabar was the usual colour for the background.

claims.text: Colours are then applied to the figures one after another, the body colours of the deities following their Dhyanamantra.

quotes.quote: Colours are applied to the figures in the next step. Consequently one colour follows the other
The body colours of different deities are painted as per their 'Dhyanamantra'.

claims.text: Ornamentation follows, colouring ornaments, head-dresses, sari borders, weapons and attributes, and white or safeda is painted to bring out their details.

quotes.quote: ornamentation is done after this. It includes colouring the ornaments, head-dresses, border of soris, weapons and attributes.
Safeda or white is painted to accentuate the intricate beauty of the ornaments and bring out the details of carving.

claims.text: Rangalekha, red lining over the ornaments, is done to stabilise the effects produced by the white ornamentation.

lede.text: Orissa Pattachitra is patta painting, one of the typical regional arts of the coastal state of Orissa, painted on a canvas of old cotton cloth pasted in layers with tamarind glue.

It was traditionally practised only by the Chitrakara caste and focuses on the Hindu epics and the Jagannath cult; while the temple images are away, three of its paintings of the trinity are kept in the main shrine as their proxies.

MAP Academy wrote in 2022 that the tradition is concentrated in Raghurajpur, and the GI application places the original centre in Puri district, in Raghurajpur and Dhandasahi on opposite banks of the Bhargavi river.

The GI application specifies vegetable and mineral colours, among them conch-shell white, lamp black, hingula or cinnabar red and haritala yellow, but sources differ on whether natural colours are still used.

sentences.text: The GI application argues that the art's primitive style and its role in temple services, contemporary with the 12th-century building of the Jagannath temple, suggest an early date, and says pata paintings flourished in Orissa in the early 15th and 16th centuries.
According to the Jagannath temple chronicle, Anangabhima Deva II first brought the Chitrakaras to Puri to do the temple's painting and gave them tax-free lands.

Every year on Jyeshtha purnima the bath discolours the wooden images of Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra, which are repainted over 15 days away from the inner sanctuary while three paintings of the trinity called anasara patti take their place.

Chitrakara society is divided into three badas named after the trinity, which supply the anasara pattis and colour the images and their cars, though Swarajya reports only two families in that service, one for Jagannath and one for Balabhadra and Subhadra.
In the remote past the paintings were made on primed paper for pilgrims, who took these jatripattis home as souvenirs, and in course of time the Chitrakaras used primed cloth.
A V&A painting of the Jagannatha temple in the Orissan style, dated 1670, was most probably executed at Puri, though the same record also says it was painted in Bhaktapur, Nepal.
After a two-year INTACH project from 1998 to 2000, Raghurajpur was selected as the first heritage village of Odisha.
The GI application gives four steps in order: preparation of patta, preparation of pigments, motif selection and layout, and finally painting.
Layers of old, used cotton cloth are pasted together with tamarind glue, smeared on in the manner of cow dung, then dried in the sun, rolled and kept.
Sources differ on how long the tamarind seeds are soaked for the glue: half a day, overnight, or 4-5 days.
The canvas is coated with khadi, tamarind glue mixed with chalk, in equal parts in the GI application but 400 gm of glue per kg of chalk in Tripathy's account.

When the coat is a bit dry it is rubbed with barada stones, jhuna barada first in the GI application but a rough khadada barada first in other sources, then a fine chikana barada, on both sides of the pati until the surface is completely polished.
In the Puri-area method the border is marked first, the sketch is made, the background is coloured, usually red, and colours are applied to the figures.
Ornaments are coloured and highlighted with white, thick black lines are given to hair and garment borders, and the master craftsman draws the fine black lines.
The finished painting is held over a charcoal fire and lacquered, which makes it water resistant and durable with a shining finish.
The GI application specifies vegetable and mineral colours, and Tripathy writes that the colours were traditionally prepared at home within the Chitrakara family.
Sources differ on present-day use: Tripathy found artists preferring enamels or watercolours, and Gulf News reports chemical-based dyes and paints for mass production.
White is prepared from conch shells, easily available on the seacoasts of Orissa, and is the basic colour from which the values of the others are determined.
The vermilion red is hingula or cinnabar and the brick red is geru or red ochre, and yellow comes from the stone haritala, identified as orpiment.
Sources differ on blue, obtained from indigo according to MAP Academy and from a stone called khandaneela according to Kiran Pradeep.
Tripathy counts six basic colours for the triad, while Kiran Pradeep writes of five main colours known as Pancha-Tatva.
Tassar cloth is one of the most popular alternatives to primed cloth, and tassar paintings are lighter and take less space.
Hingula is a red sulphide of mercury, also known as cinnabar.
Crude cinnabar is levigated in a mortar with sugar water or lime juice and the yellowish water drained off, the process being repeated fifteen times or more for the purest cinnabar.
The GI application describes orpiment as a sulphide arsenic acid found in nature as stone, a light, vivid yellow, more often slightly inclined towards orange, with a mica-like sparkle.
Gum is used in all the colours to make them sticky and permanent, and lacquering is treated as a further binding medium.

Chitrakaras are found all over the 24 feudatory states of Orissa wherever there is a Jagannath temple, and apart from Sonepur, Cuttack, Athagarh, Chikiti and Parlakhemundi their highest concentrations are at Raghurajpur and Puri.
Raghurajpur lies in Malatipatpur gram panchayat of Puri Sadar tehsil in Puri district, on the southern bank of the river Bhargavi.
Sources put Raghurajpur 10 to 14 km from Puri and 46 to 60 km from Bhubaneswar.
The GI application says that when Jagannath temples were created in other provinces, some of the painters moved to those centres.
The Orissa State Cooperative Handicrafts Corporation filed GI application 88 on 9 April 2007, and the registry issued certificate 70 on 10 July 2008.
The registry lists the registration as valid up to 8 April 2027, and its list of authorised users runs to serial number 26.
In Tripathy's 1998 study Raghurajpur had 106 Chitrakaras, 21.41% of the local population.
Tripathy also found the non-Chitrakaras practising the craft as a source of livelihood more than twice as many as the Chitrakaras.
Counts of Raghurajpur's families differ: approximately 130 in Kiran Pradeep's 2022 article, 145 in Gulf News and 100 or so households in The Better India.
Customers shifted from lower and lower-middle income pilgrims to upper-middle or upper income tourists, who are generally willing to pay a higher price.
As production came to exceed demand, competition developed between artisans and middlemen became involved, often to the artisans' disadvantage.
Themes range from Krishna's life and the avatars of Vishnu to the Ramayana and Mahabharata, and Vaishnava episodes form the major theme.
Generally all goddesses are painted yellow and the gods white; Tripathy has Krishna always painted blue, while an artist quoted by Kiran Pradeep says black and blue fill Krishna's figures.
Figures are drawn mostly in front pose with faces in profile, the elongated eyes drawn frontally, the nose long and beak-like and the chin round.
Background trees and foliage are painted over the red ground in yellow and white.
Ganjapa are circular paintings 1.2-2 cm in diameter that were used as playing cards in earlier times.
